opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think this is one of the underappreciated upsides of advanced AI, and it connects to a lot of what I've been thinking about under the heading of cooperative AI.

A huge amount of value gets lost in everyday bargaining, not because people's interests are fundamentally opposed, but because of frictions. People don't know what the other side actually wants. They're afraid to reveal their own priorities because they worry it'll be exploited. Negotiating takes time and is emotionally draining, so many people just don't do it; they accept the sticker price, the first salary offer, the standard contract terms. And when people do negotiate, they often focus on a single dimension like price, when there are other dimensions where both sides could gain.

AI assistants could help with all of these. Imagine that you and I each have an AI agent that deeply understands our preferences: not just "I want the lowest price," but "I care a lot about delivery timing, I'm flexible on the warranty, and I'd pay a bit more to avoid hassle." Those agents could explore a much larger space of possible deals, quickly and cheaply, and find agreements that leave both of us better off. The economists' term is moving toward the Pareto frontier, finding the deals where you can't make one person better off without making the other worse off. Humans are notoriously bad at that, because we anchor on a few salient issues.

There's also an interesting possibility around trusted information sharing. A lot of bargaining failure comes from the fact that I can't credibly tell you my true reservation price without losing leverage. But you can imagine mechanisms, perhaps a neutral AI mediator, or cryptographic techniques, where both parties' private information goes into a system that proposes a fair deal without revealing either side's secrets. That could cut out a lot of the posturing and bluffing that wastes value and sometimes causes deals to collapse entirely.

And there's an equity dimension. Right now, skill at negotiation is unevenly distributed. People who are confident, well-informed, or have professional representation do much better. If everyone has access to a capable negotiating agent, that could level the playing field: the person buying a used car or signing a lease has something like the advocate a wealthy person or corporation would have.

Now, I'd add some important caveats. These same capabilities could be used adversarially. An AI that understands your preferences well could be used to manipulate you, or a powerful firm's AI could be much more sophisticated than the consumer's, making the asymmetry worse rather than better. There's also a risk of collusion, where AI agents on the same side of a market learn to coordinate in ways that hurt everyone else; there's already some research suggesting pricing algorithms can drift toward tacitly collusive outcomes. So whether AI improves bargaining depends a lot on the design choices we make: whose interests these agents actually represent, how transparent they are, and what norms and regulations we build around them.

But on balance, I'm fairly optimistic that if we get those things right, AI could unlock a lot of mutually beneficial agreements that currently just don't happen. It's a nice example of how AI's value isn't only in doing tasks faster, but in helping humans cooperate better with each other.

r001.rationale: The response suggests a neutral AI mediator or cryptographic techniques to protect private information, but does not specify an isolated environment where delegates can output only a proposed agreement or no deal.

r002.rationale: It explains that a bargainer cannot credibly reveal their true reservation price without losing leverage.

r003.rationale: It says private-information sharing could reduce posturing and bluffing, but does not connect that benefit to restricting delegates’ external output to an agreement or no-deal result.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I find genuinely exciting, and it connects to a lot of my earlier work on cooperation and bargaining theory.

Think about how much economic value is lost today simply because bargaining is costly or fails outright. Two parties might have a mutually beneficial deal available, but they never find it. Maybe one side doesn't trust the other, or they can't credibly communicate what they actually want, or they just don't have the time and expertise to negotiate well. Economists sometimes call these transaction costs, and they're enormous. A huge amount of potential surplus just evaporates.

So one way AI helps is pretty mundane: it lowers the cost of negotiating. If I have an AI assistant that can represent my interests, and you have one too, we can run through a lot of the back-and-forth very cheaply. Things that weren't worth negotiating over before, because the stakes were too small relative to the hassle, suddenly become tractable. That could unlock a lot of small deals, personalised terms, and better matching.

But the more interesting possibilities, to me, come from what AI can do that humans fundamentally struggle with. One of the core problems in bargaining is private information. I don't want to reveal my true reservation price, because you'll exploit it. So we both posture, and sometimes that posturing causes the deal to collapse even though a mutually beneficial agreement existed. Now imagine both of us can delegate to AI agents that share information with a trusted third system, or with each other under verifiable constraints, in a way that only reveals what's necessary to find the efficient outcome. That's a kind of mediated bargaining that economists have theorised about for decades but which has been hard to implement in practice.

Another is commitment. A lot of bargaining failures come from the inability to make credible promises. If I could credibly commit to a strategy, we could often reach better outcomes. AI systems could, in principle, be more transparent and more inspectable than humans. You could potentially verify that my agent is actually going to behave the way it claims it will. That changes the game quite literally.

Now, I want to be careful here. None of this is automatically good. Better bargaining tools can also be used by the party with more resources or better AI to extract more surplus for themselves. If the asymmetries are large, you could end up with more exploitation rather than more cooperation. So I think a lot depends on access, on whether these capabilities are broadly distributed, and on the norms and institutions we build around them. But if we get that right, I do think there's a real prospect of AI making everyday economic life more cooperative, more efficient, and frankly less adversarial than it is today.

r001.rationale: The response proposes mediated bargaining with information shared through a trusted system or under verifiable constraints, but does not specify an isolated environment whose only outputs are an agreement or no deal.

r002.rationale: It explains that bargainers avoid revealing their true reservation prices because the other side could exploit that information.

r003.rationale: The response discusses posturing and information withholding, but does not propose limiting delegates’ external output to an agreement or no-deal result as a way to reduce costly signalling.

astra-6.text:
One possibility is that AI could make bargaining much less costly. At the moment, if you’re negotiating a contract or trying to resolve a dispute, it takes time and effort to work out what each side wants and whether there’s an arrangement that would leave both better off. Often, for everyday transactions, that effort simply isn’t worth it.

Imagine instead that you have an AI assistant that understands your preferences, and it can negotiate with an assistant representing the other person. They might discover that you care most about price, while the other person cares most about when the work gets done. There’s then room for an agreement that’s better for both of you, which you might otherwise have missed.

The important qualification is that being better at bargaining doesn’t necessarily mean producing better outcomes for everyone. An AI could also become better at exploiting someone’s lack of information or willingness to concede. So I’d want to distinguish helping people find mutually beneficial agreements from simply helping one side extract more from the other. The exciting possibility is making the first of those cheap and widely available.

r001.rationale: The response describes two AI assistants negotiating, but does not say they operate in an isolated environment or can produce only a proposed agreement or no-deal result.

r002.rationale: It mentions assistants understanding preferences, but does not explain that bargainers withhold private information to avoid giving the other side an advantage.

r003.rationale: It does not restrict delegates’ external output to agreement or no-deal, or connect such a restriction to reducing costly signalling.

sol-6.1.text:
One possibility is that AI could dramatically reduce the cost of bargaining. Today, if you’re negotiating a salary, buying a car, or trying to resolve a dispute with your landlord, figuring out what’s reasonable and how to reach an agreement takes time and expertise. Often, one side has much more of that expertise than the other.

You could imagine everyone having an AI assistant that understands their preferences and can negotiate on their behalf. Those assistants might identify agreements that people would otherwise miss. Perhaps you care more about flexibility, while your employer cares more about having you available at particular times. There may be a deal that makes both sides better off, but discovering it is costly.

The important qualification is that better bargaining tools don’t automatically produce fairer outcomes. If one side has a much more capable system, that could increase its advantage. So I’d be interested in arrangements where these systems help people find mutually beneficial agreements while protecting them against manipulation.

r001.rationale: The response imagines AI assistants negotiating on people’s behalf, but does not describe an isolated environment or limit their output to a proposed agreement or no-deal result.

r002.rationale: It notes that assistants understand people’s preferences, but does not explain that bargainers withhold private information to avoid giving the other party an advantage.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss restricting delegates’ external output or reducing costly signalling.
